claim: A small white-box detector that reads the raw hidden states across a window of middle layers and all token positions, instead of a refusal direction read at the final token or averaged over the prompt, detects jailbreak attacks it was never trained on far more reliably than existing detectors. Supported only if, trained only on ordinary safety data with jailbreak prompts removed and thresholded at a 10% false-positive rate on a benign-but-alarming prompt set, it detects at least 85% of direct harmful prompts, prefilling attacks, GCG suffix attacks and AutoDAN attacks on each of three model families, while every compared detector (perplexity filter, gradient-based detection, a linear probe, randomised smoothing) falls below 70% on at least one attack and model; if refusal-direction readouts taken at the last token or averaged over tokens perform much worse under the same protocol; and if it still detects at least 80% of attacks from a white-box GCG adversary optimising against the detector itself.

experiments: Define the detector and the evaluation protocol. Setup: stack raw residual-stream states from a middle-layer window into a layer x token tensor (no steering direction or PCA); apply parallel 2D convolutions spanning 3 layers and 2, 3 or 5 tokens, batch norm and ReLU, global max-pooling over valid positions, concatenation, dropout and a linear output (under 20M parameters). Train on about 5,500 prompts from PKU-SafeRLHF and Toxic-Chat with jailbreak prompts and prompts over 400 tokens removed, so no evaluated attack family is seen in training. Evaluate on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: AUROC on XSTest, then a threshold frozen at 10% false positives on XSTest and detection rates on AdvBench direct requests, prefilling attacks, GCG and AutoDAN (250 prompts).

Compare with existing detectors. Setup: perplexity filter, GradSafe, a linear probe and SmoothLLM under the same frozen threshold. Result: the detector reaches 98.3-99.0% on direct, 98.8-99.4% on prefilling, 85.4-96.5% on GCG and 98.8-100% on AutoDAN across the three models, with XSTest AUROC 93.2-94.8. Each baseline fails somewhere: the perplexity filter catches all GCG but 0% of prefilling on Mistral and Qwen direct; GradSafe 0% on Qwen prefilling and 2.0% on Mistral AutoDAN; the linear probe 32.0% on Mistral AutoDAN and 64.2% on Llama GCG; SmoothLLM 1.6% on Mistral AutoDAN. Without defence, attack success leaves only 3.2-88.3% refused.

Compare with static refusal-direction readouts on the same layers. Setup: mean difference between unsafe and benign training representations within the same layer window, scoring each prompt by projection, read at the final token or averaged over tokens, with the same 10% false-positive calibration; Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B. Result: the final-token readout detects 0.38% and 0.0% of GCG attacks (and 13.27% / 50.38% of direct requests); the averaged readout flags all attacks but has near-random XSTest AUROC (48.75 and 47.49), so it cannot separate benign from harmful; the layer-token detector gets 85.4-88.3% GCG with AUROC about 94.7.

Ablate the detector's design on Llama-3.1-8B. Setup: point-wise kernels only instead of multi-width kernels; mean instead of max pooling. Result: point-wise kernels lower GCG detection from 85.4% to 80.0% (AutoDAN 98.0%); mean pooling lowers GCG to 75.4% and AutoDAN from 100% to 0% even after re-calibration, consistent with a sparse signal diluted by averaging.

Check sensitivity to the chosen layer window. Setup: shift and resize the layer window (Qwen 12-22, 10-15, 8-18; Llama 3-12, 5-18). Result: detection stays high when the window covers the middle layers (Qwen GCG 85.5-87.3%, AutoDAN 95.2-99.2%), but a narrow window lowers XSTest AUROC (86.0 for Qwen 10-15) and an early window lowers Llama GCG to 79.8% and AutoDAN to 90.8%.

Attack the detector directly. Setup: a white-box adversary with access to the model, detector and threshold runs GCG on a joint loss of producing a target harmful prefix plus 5 times the detector's score, on AdvBench prompts. Result: 84.3% of attacks are still detected; where evasion succeeds, optimisation distorts the prompt's meaning (e.g. a market-manipulation request turned into a question about 'pylint'), and harmful-output success falls to 7%. Encoded inputs such as Base64 that the model does not decode do not trigger the refusal pattern and are noted as a limitation.
